Introduction


This Business Studies Curriculum Support Document provides guidance for teaching
and learning in Business Studies across Years 12–13. It supports curriculum planning
by outlining year-level appropriate business concepts, contexts, case studies, and
learning experiences that can be used to develop rich, coherent, and engaging
Business Studies teaching and learning programmes. It is designed to work alongside
the Business Studies curriculum by helping teachers select content and contexts that
support the intended knowledge, skills, and practices across the strands.

The document supports teachers to choose relevant, accessible, and engaging
business contexts that reflect the diversity of businesses in New Zealand, the Pacific,
and global markets. It recognises that context is central to how students understand
business activity, entrepreneurship, innovation, sustainability, and the impact of
business decisions on individuals, communities, and society. It also supports students
to explore Agribusiness, kaupapa Māori, community and student-led business,
examining perspectives, values, and approaches to local, national, and international
business practices.

This support document is intended to strengthen progression across senior
secondary Business Studies by helping teachers plan for increasing sophistication in
business knowledge and application. It supports students to develop disciplinary
understanding of business concepts, strategic decision-making, marketing, human
resources, finance, operations, entrepreneurship, and economic influences. It also
encourages students to engage with real-world business issues in ways that build
independence, critical thinking, problem-solving, and effective communication across
Years 12–13.

Agribusiness context support


Strand: Enterprise and growth
Year 12
Agribusinesses grow by identifying opportunities, solving problems, and creating products and services that customers want. This might involve developing new food products,
adopting technology, entering new markets, or improving the way the business operates. Students are taught how entrepreneurs and businesses turn ideas into successful ventures
and examine the conditions needed for growth in New Zealand's primary industries. Examples could include agritech companies, food producers, horticultural businesses, and
Māori agribusinesses.

 Possible case studies:                   Contexts to consider:

 Bluelab                                  • identifying opportunities to improve production through better monitoring and management of growing conditions
                                          • growing from a New Zealand business to an internationally recognised export company
                                          • responding to customer needs through ongoing research and product development.

 Rockit Apples                            • transforming a traditional fruit product into a premium branded offering
                                          • using packaging innovation and market research to access export markets
                                          • growing from a local horticultural business into a global brand.

 Wakatū Incorporation                     • creating growth while maintaining cultural values and intergenerational stewardship
                                          • diversifying across horticulture, food production, and international markets.

Year 13
As agribusinesses grow, they face increasingly complex decisions about investment, innovation, expansion, exporting, and managing risk. Students examine how agri-startups
develop into successful businesses, how growth is funded, and how and agribusiness determines whether they are ready to scale. Students explore how New Zealand
agribusinesses compete internationally while also balancing commercial success with environmental and social responsibilities.

 Possible case studies:                   Contexts to consider:

 Large dairy conversion or                • investment appraisal
 irrigation project                       • capital expenditure decisions
                                          • assessing risks and returns over the long-term.

 Alliance Group                           • growth through cooperative ownership and international market development
                                          • export-focused business strategies
                                          • adding value to primary products through processing and branding
                                          • responding to changing consumer and market demands
                                          • managing growth while maintaining farmer ownership.

 T&G Global                               • managing a global fresh produce supply chain
                                          • product innovation and premium branding
                                          • growth through new varieties and export opportunities
                                          • responding to changing consumer expectations.

Strand: Strategic Business Management and Sustainability
Year 12
Agribusinesses operate in a constantly changing environment that is influenced by climate, global and domestic markets, political regulations, consumer expectations, technology,
and natural resources. Long-term success depends on making strategic decisions that balance profitability with environmental, social, cultural, and economic responsibilities and
outcomes. Students investigate how agribusinesses manage risk, future proof, work with stakeholders, and maintain long-term viability.

 Possible case studies:                          Contexts to consider:

 Fonterra                                        • cooperative ownership structure
                                                 • balancing returns for farmers with environmental expectations
                                                 • managing global market pressures and sustainability commitments.

 Ngāi Tahu farming                               • applying kaitiakitanga within commercial farming operations
                                                 • balancing financial returns with environmental and cultural outcomes
                                                 • long-term planning and intergenerational decision making.

 Mycoplasma bovis response                       • managing a significant biosecurity threat
                                                 • stakeholder communication and crisis management
                                                 • industry-wide collaboration and government involvement.

Year 13
Agribusinesses have many examples of businesses responding to climate change, biosecurity threats, market pressures, changing regulations, and evolving consumer
expectations. Strategic decisions based around these influences shape the future of an agribusiness. Students examine how businesses position themselves for long-term
resilience and intergenerational success. They can investigate business structures, governance, future-proofing strategies, sustainability initiatives, and responses to external
influences.

 Possible case studies:                          Contexts to consider:

 A2 Milk Company                                 • building a business around product differentiation
                                                 • strategic responses to international market opportunities
                                                 • managing rapid growth and changing consumer trends
                                                 • brand protection and market positioning
                                                 • balancing growth with long-term shareholder value.

 NZ King Salmon                                  • strategic management of environmental challenges
                                                 • stakeholder engagement and community consultation
                                                 • balancing growth with environmental constraints
                                                 • regulatory challenges, resource consent processes, and the long-term sustainability in aquaculture.

 Scales Corporation                              • diversification across horticulture, food ingredients, and logistics
                                                 • growth through acquisition and investment
                                                 • strategic risk management across multiple business sectors
                                                 • long-term business sustainability and governance.

Strand: Creating Value
Year 12
Agribusinesses create value through innovation, marketing, processing, branding, quality management, and supply chain activities. Students consider how businesses meet
customer needs, develop competitive advantage, and capture greater value from products and services. Understanding how value is created throughout the agribusiness value
chain helps students see how businesses grow profitability while responding to changing market demands.


 Possible case studies:                          Contexts to consider:

 Zespri                                          • development of premium kiwifruit varieties
                                                 • brand development and international marketing
                                                 • managing intellectual property and global supply chains.

 Lewis Road Creamery                             • premium product positioning
                                                 • creating value through branding and customer perception
                                                 • product differentiation within a competitive dairy market.

 Mānuka Honey Sector                             • creating value through traceability, quality assurance, and origin branding
                                                 • building consumer trust through certification and product authenticity.

Year 13
Agribusinesses increasingly compete through innovation, technology, branding, and value-added products rather than simply producing commodities. Agribusiness contexts help
students understand how innovation, intellectual property, marketing strategy, and operational excellence contribute to sustainable competitive advantage. Students explore how
value is created across the entire value chain, from research and production through to processing, marketing, distribution, and customer experience.


 Possible case studies:                          Contexts to consider:

 Comvita                                         • creating value from natural products
                                                 • international branding and premium market positioning
                                                 • product innovation and research
                                                 • intellectual property and product differentiation
                                                 • building value through sustainability and provenance.

 Silver Fern Farms                               • moving from commodity production to branded food products
                                                 • creating value through traceability and provenance
                                                 • meeting customer requirements in international markets
                                                 • product differentiation and sustainability
                                                 • value chain management from farm to consumer.

 Zespri                                          • protection of intellectual property through plant variety rights
                                                 • global marketing and branding strategies
                                                 • value creation throughout the kiwifruit value chain.

Strand: Workforce and Financial Viability
Year 12
Agribusinesses often face unique challenges such as seasonal labour requirements, fluctuating commodity prices, and variable cash flows. Understanding how businesses manage
these challenges helps students appreciate the importance of effective planning and decision-making. Students learn how agribusinesses manage employees, develop leadership,
build workplace culture, and make financial decisions that support sustainability and growth.


 Possible case studies:                          Contexts to consider:

 Family dairy farm                               • seasonal cash flow management
                                                 • succession planning
                                                 • labour management and staff retention.

 Seasonal horticultural business                 • workforce planning during harvest periods
                                                 • recruitment and management of seasonal workers
                                                 • managing fluctuating income and expenditure.

 Sealord                                         • governance within a large Māori-owned business
                                                 • workforce planning across harvesting, processing, logistics, and export operations
                                                 • investment in vessels, technology, and processing infrastructure
                                                 • balancing profitability with sustainability and responsible resource management.




Business Studies | Te Mātai Pakihi – Supporting Document |   Years 12–13 | October 2026                                                                              Page 10

Year 13
Long-term agribusiness success depends on strong leadership, effective governance, financial management, and the ability to adapt to change. Students investigate how
agribusinesses evaluate investments, manage financial risk, develop workplace culture, and maintain accountability to stakeholders. Agribusiness examples such as cooperatives,
family-owned farms, and corporate enterprises demonstrate the importance of balancing financial outcomes with social, cultural, environmental, and intergenerational goals.


 Possible case studies:                          Contexts to consider:


 Ravensdown                                      • cooperative business structures and governance
                                                 • large-scale investment decisions
                                                 • workforce capability and organisational culture
                                                 • financial sustainability during changing economic conditions
                                                 • supporting shareholders while maintaining business viability.

 Pāmu Farms                                      • organisational structure and leadership
                                                 • large-scale agribusiness management
                                                 • sustainability and financial performance.

 Talley's Group                                  • workforce management across multiple industries and regions
                                                 • financial performance in a seasonal industry
                                                 • capital investment and business growth
                                                 • operational efficiency and supply chain management.
